# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: The look-back window (screen 4) sits between two context screens that carry the same heading and question (3 and 5), so the context step is split around it rather than finished first.

screens.why2: The rivals are plain cluster talk to me (partition, queue, GPU-hour allocation), but my own row ends in a stray 'yours', so 'Stopping a job failing partway through yours' needs a second read and would sound garbled read aloud.
screens.why3: Every row is something a researcher on a SLURM or K8s cluster deals with at submit time: sizing, picking a partition, staging data, getting software built, checking the allocation.
screens.why4: The four rivals are distinct and in our words, but the own row is odd: it has the trailing 'yours' and covers only the failing half of my problem, not the waste.
screens.why5: My problem is guessing sizes so a job neither dies mid-run nor sits on idle GPUs; 'Stopping a job failing partway through' keeps only the under-request half and drops the over-request waste that is the core of Expanse's pitch.
screens.why7: The shape holds (own row first, four rivals, none a part or cause of another, belief testable both ways), but the own row is narrowed to one half of the pair, against the card's 'both halves kept', and carries a stray word.
screens.instead: Own row: 'Sizing a job so it neither fails nor wastes GPUs', then 'Choosing which partition or queue to submit to', 'Moving data on and off the cluster', 'Getting software working on the cluster', 'Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation before submitting'.

screens.why1: After the importance check, asking how researchers size jobs today and how that goes is the obvious next step before testing whether today's way falls short.
screens.why2: The question uses my own job words, and the hint's example makes clear I should name the one step and its means, which I can answer straight away: guessing sizes and padding them.
screens.why3: How researchers guess and over-request before submitting to SLURM or K8s is exactly what we measured across 122k jobs, so I answer from what I know.
screens.why4: The only option is the I'm-not-sure chip, which fits a founder's answer screen, and the two boxes take the act and the rungs cleanly.
screens.why5: What I typed, guessing and requesting two to three times so jobs don't die mid-run, rungs graded by how much sat idle, is held word for word.
screens.why7: The first box gives the act and its means in under 25 words; the second gives three rungs on the one measure of reserved-versus-used, with a working first rung; the line defaults under it, leaving Keel to add two worse rungs on the same measure.

screens.why1: Right after I said how researchers size jobs today, checking the five ways that sizing turned out is the obvious next step, and it does not repeat the earlier failure-count screens.
screens.why2: 'Ran first time', 'holding twice what it used' and 'failed partway and had to be resubmitted' are how anyone who submits to SLURM talks about a job.
screens.why3: A researcher knows whether their last job died, got resubmitted or ran, and roughly how much of its request it used from sacct or seff.
screens.why4: The rungs run in order and cover the usual cases, but 'Never ran to the end' partly overlaps 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' (a job that was resubmitted and died again fits both), and a job padded to about 1.5 times falls between 'about right' and 'about twice'.
screens.why5: It keeps my two failure modes, over-requesting by two to three times and under-requesting so the job dies mid-run, and my line under 'sized about right', since a 2x pad is exactly the waste I sell against.
screens.why7: There are five rungs, best to worst, with a working first rung, the line under it and the bar naming it, so the belief can go either way; but the last two rungs grade whether the job ran rather than how much it held idle, which is the stand-in the card itself cites ('Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' under three rungs of idle reservation), so the one-measure rule is bent.
screens.instead: How did sizing your last job go? Ran first time, sized about right · Ran, holding about twice what it used · Ran, holding three times or more what it used · Ran out of memory or time and had to be resubmitted · Never finished, even after resubmitting · I can't recall

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is the obvious last step before the study goes out to researchers, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Two named voices with a five-second preview are plain on first read; the credits line is Keel's own billing word, but it is stated clearly.
screens.why3: I know the researchers on our clusters well enough to pick which voice they would sit through, and I can hear both before choosing.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a preview, and a default already picked, so no option is missing or overlapping for a choice of taste.
screens.why5: It still says researchers, as I typed it, and nothing about Expanse, agents or clusters leaks into a choice of voice.
screens.instead: Same screen, but let me send the link by email or a Slack/Teams message as well as text, since that is how researchers on a shared cluster are actually reached.

screens.why1: Once I've picked who asks the questions, choosing how researchers answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words, and each option says exactly what the respondent will do, so I can pick on first read.
screens.why3: I know my researchers sit at terminals and would rather tap through a short form between submissions than talk to a video, so I can answer from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete: the AI interviewer, text, or letting them pick; the last one doubles as the 'not sure' choice.
screens.why5: Nothing about my product or my roles is changed here; it only asks about the format, and it keeps my segment's words.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how they answer, the last step is naturally who receives a link, so it lands exactly where I expect it.
screens.why2: Three plain routes, by name, from a Contacts search, or one open link posted where people gather, are clear on first read to a founder doing outreach.
screens.why3: I know whether I am sending to researchers I know personally, a list I built, or posting into a Slack or HPC user forum, so this is mine to answer.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the Keel-search option's description runs long and mixes how lists work into the label, and there is no mixed option for someone who would both send named links and post an open one.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product, roles or wording is restated or bent here; it is purely about distribution, and my pick of named people is shown as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (one link each) / A list from a Contacts search (one link each) / Everyone in a group I post one open link to (they sign in with Google).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 counted', but the threshold that decides it (5 needed) only appears down on the cards, and the line names only Frequency when Importance and Current solution are short by the same margin.
screens.why_b2: No chart here, but the tally (1 holding, 3 too few, 7 answered) and each card's '4 counted · 5 needed' or '6 of 7 · bar 6 of 7' make the count, the base and the bar plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: My problem is that everyone over-requests two to three times and wastes the cluster, yet Prevalence and Frequency are phrased around a job failing partway, the under-request half of my line; recognisable, but tilted away from the waste I lead with.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page tells me what to do; I have to infer from '5 needed' that one more counted answer on three cards would settle them, and 'What it measures' only explains the rule.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible everywhere, the short counts are called too few rather than leaned on, and Prevalence holding at exactly 6 of 7 is shown as 'at the bar', not as strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: Frequency, Importance and Current solution each had 4 of the 5 answers needed, while Prevalence held at exactly the bar (6 of 7). Get one more researcher who submitted jobs this week to answer before reading these, and note the cards test failed jobs, not the over-requesting you lead with.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I see both that it held and that it held by exactly the one person it needed.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against on a 0-to-7 axis, with my bar marked at 6, so what is counted, out of how many, and where the bar sits are all clear at first look.
screens.why_b3: My band 'at least 8 in 10' is kept, but the belief now reads 'had a job fail partway through', and my segment loses 'on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs'; my problem is that everyone pads requests to avoid failure and wastes the cluster, so a mid-run failure is one face of it, not the thing I counted at 8 in 10.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' points me onward, but it says nothing about what a mid-run failure in 6 of 7 researchers means for selling predicted job sizes.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n=7 visible, calls this 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and says 'at your bar exactly' rather than claiming strength, though the stray '— the most recent time it happened' after a yes/no question is a puzzling tail.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 researchers on 100+ GPU SLURM/K8s clusters had a job fail partway in the last 5 working days: 6 of 7 said yes, exactly at your bar, a lean from 7 people; next see whether the rest pad their requests instead, which is the waste you sell against.

screens.why_b1: The status "Too few to call" sits right beside its deciding number, "4 counted · 5 needed to call it", and the So line repeats the two together.
screens.why_b2: What is counted (working days out of 5) and the n are plain, but the bar takes a second look: the strip's "your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)" sits next to 4 counted, all of them for, so at first glance it reads as if the bar is already met, the 0 tick shows an answer nobody could give, and the legend has a "short of it" with nothing in it.
screens.why_b3: The 3 to 5 working days out of 5 is mine, but "have a job fail partway through" is only one side of my problem (the over-requesting and idle GPUs are the bigger part), and "Researchers and ML engineers" is my segment's wording, not the researchers who run jobs on shared GPU clusters I wrote.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it does not say that one more counted answer decides it, or that all four counted so far are at my low or above.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, the two not counted named with their reasons), and the small group is flagged as "a lean, not a call" rather than a hold.
screens.instead: All 4 researchers counted had a job fail partway on 3 or more of the last 5 working days; I need 4 of 5 counted at 3 or more, so one more counted answer decides it. Ask one more researcher before reading anything into this.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats the same thing, so I know where I stand and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts 8 picks over 4 people, and my row is marked with 3 for, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' next to '4 counted' takes a second look before I see it means 4 of the 5 people the call needs.
screens.why_b3: I can recognise my problem, but it has been cut to 'Stopping a job failing partway through', which drops the half I care about most, sizing so the job neither fails nor wastes GPUs; the belief also opens on the segment wording rather than my 'researchers who run jobs on shared GPU clusters'.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer decides it, or that 3 of 4 already put it in their two.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the two uncounted people and the reason for each are named, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps the 3-of-4 from being read as a result.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 counted put failing partway in their two (the bar is 4 of 5), so one more counted researcher decides it. Note that the row you named was narrowed from 'sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the number that decides it, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the 'below here, today's way fell short' line read at once, but the strip 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a ghost cell and a marker at 4 took me a second look to see it means 4 of 5 would be needed once a fifth answer is in.
screens.why_b3: It is my belief in my words: my segment ('researchers and ML engineers'), my act of guessing memory, time and GPUs before submitting, and the bar names the rung I chose, 'Ran first time, sized about right'.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me that 3 of the 4 counted fell short, or that one more counted answer would let it be called.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, with reasons for the two left out) and the low n is said plainly ('a small group: a lean, not a call') with no claim beyond it.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 counted fell short of 'Ran first time, sized about right'; one more counted researcher decides it, so send it to a few more.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', but the box's own count is '1 against · 1 asked their why here', and the screen never says how that one answer bears on the verdict.
screens.why_b3: Importance and 'Stopping a job failing partway through' are my belief, but the five-things framing and the long circumstance clause are Keel's restatement and not the line I typed.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next, such as recruiting more researchers or probing whether data movement and software setup outrank sizing for engineers who already size from past runs.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible (4 of 5 needed, 1 against, 1 asked) and the group is labelled 'On their own (1)', so nothing is claimed beyond one person.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's quote tells me something I did not write: for an engineer who sizes from last week's runs, moving data and getting libraries to agree is where the day goes, which is a real rival for the pain I am selling against.
screens.instead: Too few to call (4 of 5); the one researcher against already sizes from past runs and spends the day on data movement and software setup, so recruit more and ask whether sizing still outranks those once sizes come from history.

screens.why1: As the first screen, asking whether my cluster is big enough is an obvious gate before anything about my jobs.
screens.why2: Clusters, submitting jobs and GPU counts are my everyday words, and I can answer on one read.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our shared cluster is, but someone on a cloud or a partition-limited allocation might only see their own share and have to guess the total.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and a gate takes no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 100-or-more-GPU segment without leaking any product or role words.
screens.why6: Short, one question, two options easy to hold when heard.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a cluster of 100 or more GPUs, asking whether a job of mine died mid-run this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "A job fail partway through" is exactly how I'd say it in the lab; I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which of my jobs died in the last week; it's in my squeue history and in the lost hours I had to resubmit.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is a job killed mid-run because memory or time was under-requested, but "fail partway through" also takes in my code bugs, NaN losses and node crashes, so the meaning drifted wider.
screens.why6: It is one short question with a plain "Yes or no" that I can hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The measure and shape are right (two answers, both true of someone, no escape), but the gate dropped the condition that made it the founder's problem, so a Yes counts failures that have nothing to do with guessing resources and inflates the share.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job of yours get killed partway through for running out of memory or time? Yes · No

screens.why1: I just said yes to having a job fail partway through this week, so asking on how many of those days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "A job fail partway through" and "working days" are how I'd talk about my runs, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know which days this week a run died on me; I check squeue and the logs every morning.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 5 covers every answer after a yes, and "I can't recall" is the right way out.
screens.why5: "Fail partway through" counts any crash, like a code bug or a node going down, not only jobs killed for asking too little memory, GPUs or time, so it has drifted a little from the guessing problem.
screens.why6: Heard once it's short and one question, "a number from 1 to 5" is easy to hold, and the escape comes last.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the window, from 1 to the window's 5, with no 0 and the one cant_recall escape; the founder's range isn't shown here, so I'm assuming its low is at least 2 so some buttons can count against.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 5 working days did a job get killed for running out of memory or time? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking how often a job died partway through, asking what I'd most want made easier about my runs makes sense.
screens.why2: 'Stopping a job failing partway through' needs a second read, since 'stopping a job' is what scancel does; I'd say 'stopping a job from failing'.
screens.why3: Every row is something I deal with on our cluster: picking a partition, staging data, checking our GPU-hours, fighting CUDA and module versions, and losing runs to OOM or the time limit.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and mine, but the failure row is an outcome rather than the thing I actually do, guessing memory, GPUs and wall time, so it sits oddly beside four tasks.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but the founder's hurt of having to guess the request up front has widened into 'any job failing', which also covers node faults and bugs.
screens.why6: Five short options read as a list I can hold and the one escape is said last; the allocation row is only a little long.
screens.why7: The own item is there, not first, with two-plus rivals and None of these at the first ask, but the own row is the outcome rather than the founder's act at submission (sizing the request), so a for-pick doesn't quite test the belief.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of jobs on the cluster. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Guessing a job's memory, GPUs and run time · Choosing which partition to submit to · Moving data on and off the cluster · Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation · Getting software working on the cluster · None of these

screens.why1: Right after I picked the step I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how sizing my last submission actually went.
screens.why2: Mostly my words, but 'holding about twice what it used' is odd; I'd say 'requested about twice what it used', and with three resources named I'm not sure which one 'twice' refers to.
screens.why3: I size every job myself and can check seff or sacct for what it actually used, so I can answer from my own last run.
screens.why4: 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' and 'Never ran to the end' overlap, since my failed run also never finished, and there's no rung for a mixed result like memory doubled but time about right, or for an OOM at startup.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks; 'failed partway and had to be resubmitted' is exactly the thing that costs me days, in words I'd use.
screens.why6: It's one question with five options, but 'memory, time and GPUs' plus 'holding three times or more what it used' is a mouthful to hold by ear.
screens.why7: There's a working first rung, a failed last rung and a fitting 'I can't recall', but rung 4 ('Failed partway and had to be resubmitted') sits under rungs that grade idle reservation and steps off that measure, which is the card's own named example of a stand-in.
screens.instead: Think of your last job submission. How close was what you requested to what it used? — Requested about what it used · Requested up to twice what it used · Requested three times or more · Requested too little, it got killed · It never ran at all — or I can't recall
